text: You've now seen the same Bell-state circuit give slightly different counts on different runs, even with no noise involved. That's not a quirk to shrug off — it's a predictable statistical effect with a formula behind it.

Every time you call backend.run with shots=N, the simulator or real hardware prepares the qubits from scratch, runs every gate, measures, records the outcome, and starts over — N times. Each one of those N independent repetitions is a shot, and the counts dictionary is just a tally of which bitstring came out on each one.

Consider a qubit with a true measurement probability of exactly 0.5. The observed frequency over N shots has a known standard error: the square root of p times 1 minus p, over N — standard binomial sampling theory, the same math behind polling margins of error. At 100 shots that's about 0.05, or plus-or-minus 9.8 percentage points. At 1024 shots, about 0.0156, or plus-or-minus 3.1 points. At 8192 shots, about 0.0055, or plus-or-minus 1.1 points.

Real seeded draws show the pattern. At N=100, one draw gave 47 and 53 — well within the wide band you'd expect. At N=1024, a draw landed exactly 512 and 512, right on the true value, though it easily could have come out otherwise. At N=8192, a draw gave roughly 50.85%, closer to 50% in absolute terms, consistent with the narrower band at that shot count.

Here's the pattern that matters practically: going from 100 to roughly 1024 shots, about ten times as many, cuts standard error by only about 3.2 times, not ten. This 1-over-square-root-of-N scaling means cutting your uncertainty in half takes four times the shots, not two. And shots aren't free — they cost wall-clock time on a simulator, and queue time or real cost on quantum hardware, so choosing a shot count is a genuine engineering tradeoff.
Next lesson adds a second, independent source of error on top of sampling noise: real quantum gates aren't perfect, and qiskit_aer.noise lets you model that before you ever touch real hardware.
